prompt: Ana deployed `prod`, then added `POST` to `/orders` and did nothing else. On AWS, a partner calls `POST /orders` on `prod`. What comes back?
hint: The stage serves a copy taken at one moment.

choices.text: `429 Too Many Requests`, from the usage plan
choices.why: The plan throttles calls it can route; this method is not in the deployment at all.

choices.text: `403` with `Missing Authentication Token`
choices.why: Yes. The deployment predates `POST`, and a REST API answers a method it does not have with that misleading message.

choices.text: `200` with the MOCK body, since the resource exists
choices.why: The MOCK belongs to `GET`. `POST` has no integration and is not deployed.

choices.text: `404 Not Found`, as for any unknown path
choices.why: A REST API does not answer `404` here; it answers `403`, which is why the message confuses people.

prompt: What does a deployment of a REST API hold?
hint: `get-stage` named one by its id.

choices.text: The requests the stage served since it was taken
choices.why: That is what logs and metrics record. A deployment is configuration.

choices.text: Only the methods changed since the previous deployment
choices.why: It is a whole copy, which is why pointing the stage at an older id rolls everything back.

choices.text: The resources and methods as they were at that moment
choices.why: Yes. It is a frozen copy of the tree, and a stage points at one.

choices.text: The API keys allowed to call the stage
choices.why: Keys belong to usage plans, which name stages; the deployment knows nothing of them.

prompt: Put in order what it takes for `GET /orders` on a new REST API to answer on a stage.
hint: A child needs its parent, a verb needs its path, and nothing answers before the copy.
trap: Deploying before the method exists is refused, and deploying before the integration leaves a method with nowhere to send the request.

prompt: A partner's API key turns up in a public log. With the key alone, what can a stranger do?
hint: What is the key for, according to AWS?

choices.text: Call the API as that partner, spending the partner's quota
choices.why: Yes. A key identifies a client for metering; whoever holds it is that client to API Gateway.

choices.text: Nothing, without the partner's IAM credentials as well
choices.why: The method required a key and no authoriser; nothing else is asked for.

choices.text: Change the partner's usage plan
choices.why: Plans are changed through the AWS API with the account's credentials, not with a key.

choices.text: Read the partner's data in every other API of the account
choices.why: A key works where a plan attaches it to a stage, and a method asks for it.

prompt: A REST API answers no request until a ___ of it is put on a stage.
hint: It is what `create-` followed by this word makes.

prompt: In the lab, Ana sends 50 requests a second to her `prod` stage, whose plan allows 10. What happens?
hint: Think about what moto serves at a stage's address.

choices.text: moto answers `429` after the twentieth, as AWS would
choices.why: moto stores the throttle and enforces none of it.

choices.text: moto answers all 50, because it does not throttle
choices.why: It does not throttle, but it does not answer either: there is no stage address in moto to call.

choices.text: Nothing reaches it: moto serves no stage address
choices.why: Yes. moto keeps the definitions and answers the control plane only.

choices.text: moto refuses the plan when it is created
choices.why: It accepted the plan and printed it back.

prompt: At the first-tier prices on the sheet of 16 October 2026, how much less does an HTTP API cost than a REST API in a month of 30 million requests?
hint: 4.25 and 1.59 per million.

prompt: A handler reads `event["httpMethod"]` and works behind a REST API's Lambda proxy integration. It is moved behind an HTTP API integration with payload format `2.0`. What happens?
hint: Look at where `get-order.json` keeps the method.

choices.text: It works: the two formats carry the same fields
choices.why: They differ, and the method is one of the fields that moved.

choices.text: API Gateway answers `405 Method Not Allowed`
choices.why: The route matched; the failure is inside the function.

choices.text: It raises `KeyError`; the method moved
choices.why: Yes. Format 1.0 has `httpMethod` at the top; 2.0 has `requestContext.http.method`.

choices.text: API Gateway rewrites the event into format 1.0 for it
choices.why: The integration says which format it wants and receives exactly that one.

prompt: On AWS, a request reaches `GET /orders/{id}` with a token whose `exp` passed an hour ago. What happens?
hint: The authoriser sits before the integration.

choices.text: The function runs and has to check `exp` itself
choices.why: The JWT authoriser checks `exp` for you; the function only sees tokens that passed.

choices.text: API Gateway answers `401` and the function is not called
choices.why: Yes. A token that fails a check stops at the door.

choices.text: `403` with `Missing Authentication Token`
choices.why: That is a REST API's answer for a path or method it does not have.

choices.text: The function runs with `authorizer` set to null in the event
choices.why: A route with a JWT authoriser never passes an unchecked request through.

prompt: Which of these did the lab in this section really run or show? Choose all that apply.
hint: moto serves nothing at an API's address; the emulator runs a handler.

choices.text: The handler answering the event in the real Python 3.12 runtime
choices.why: Yes: the Lambda base image ran it and printed the dictionary.

choices.text: moto storing the route with its JWT authoriser
choices.why: Yes: `create-route` printed `AuthorizationType: JWT`.

choices.text: A token checked against the issuer's public keys
choices.why: No token was ever sent; that part is AWS's documented behaviour.

choices.text: API Gateway turning `statusCode` into an HTTP status
choices.why: API Gateway was not in front of the emulator; the prose says so.

choices.text: The condition on the function's permission statement
choices.why: Yes: `add-permission` returned it, with the API's id in the source ARN.

prompt: Why does the section run `aws lambda add-permission` after creating the route?
hint: Whose policy does it change?

choices.text: Calls fail with `500`; the function never runs
choices.why: Yes. It lets API Gateway invoke the function, from this API only.

choices.text: Without it `create-route` would be refused
choices.why: The route was created before it; the permission matters at call time.

choices.text: It lets the function call API Gateway
choices.why: The other way round: the principal is `apigateway.amazonaws.com`.

choices.text: REST APIs need it; HTTP APIs reuse the function's role
choices.why: Both kinds invoke through the function's resource policy.

prompt: An HTTP API meters requests in steps of 512 KB. As how many requests is one upload of 1,300 KB billed?
hint: Round up, not to the nearest.

prompt: The `chat` API has the routes `$connect`, `$disconnect`, `$default` and `send`. A client sends `{"action": "refund", "order": 42}`. Which route runs?
hint: The selection expression reads `action`.

choices.text: `send`, the only route for messages
choices.why: `send` runs only for `"action": "send"`.

choices.text: None: API Gateway closes the connection
choices.why: With `$default` defined, an unmatched message still reaches a function.

choices.text: `$connect`, which checks every message
choices.why: `$connect` runs once, when the connection opens.

choices.text: `$default`
choices.why: Yes. No route is called `refund`, so the message falls to `$default`.

prompt: 500 clients stay connected 6 hours a day for 20 days. At 0.388 USD per million connection minutes, what do the minutes cost?
hint: Clients × hours × 60 × days.

prompt: On AWS, the backend posts to a stored connection id whose client closed the tab a second ago. What does it get, and what should it do?
hint: moto answered this case differently from AWS.

choices.text: Success, and the message waits until the client reconnects
choices.why: API Gateway keeps no mailbox; a new connection gets a new id.

choices.text: `GoneException` (410); delete the stored id and carry on
choices.why: Yes. It is how a sender learns of a close before `$disconnect` is processed.

choices.text: Exit status 0, as the lab showed
choices.why: That was moto, which accepts any id; AWS refuses an id with no connection.

choices.text: A `429`, because the connection is being closed
choices.why: 429 is throttling; a missing connection is a 410.

prompt: Match each route of the `chat` API with when it runs.
hint: Two run once per connection, two once per message.

pairs.right: once, when a client opens the connection
after the connection has closed, best effort
for a message no other route matches

right_distractors: every ten minutes, to keep the connection alive

prompt: A warehouse screen must show new orders all through an 8-hour shift over one WebSocket API. What does its client have to do?
hint: Two limits from AWS's documentation.

choices.text: Keep it busy within ten minutes, and reconnect after two hours
choices.why: Yes, and the backend stores the new connection id each time.

choices.text: Ask AWS for 8-hour connections through a quota increase on the stage
choices.why: The two-hour maximum is a fixed limit, not an adjustable quota.

choices.text: Nothing: a connection stays open for as long as its stage exists
choices.why: Connections close at two hours, and after ten silent minutes.

choices.text: Send every message to `$default` so the timer resets
choices.why: Any message resets the idle timer; the route is irrelevant, and the two-hour limit stays.

prompt: A WebSocket connection stays open for an hour and nobody sends anything. Which meter grows?
hint: One meter counts, the other times.

choices.text: Messages, counted in steps of 32 KB
choices.why: No message was sent, so there is nothing to count.

choices.text: Both, in equal parts
choices.why: Only one of them depends on time alone.

choices.text: Neither, until the first message
choices.why: The minutes start when the connection opens.

choices.text: Connection minutes
choices.why: Yes. They run for as long as the connection is open.

prompt: Which of these does a REST API offer and an HTTP API not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four rows of the table.

choices.text: Usage plans with a quota per client
choices.why: Yes; HTTP APIs have no API keys.

choices.text: A response cache on the stage
choices.why: Yes; only a REST stage caches.

choices.text: A JWT authoriser with no code of yours
choices.why: That one is the HTTP API's.

choices.text: AWS WAF in front of the API
choices.why: Yes; WAF attaches to REST stages.

choices.text: A Lambda authoriser
choices.why: Both kinds have it.

choices.text: A private endpoint reachable only from a VPC
choices.why: Yes; HTTP APIs are public.

prompt: Behind an HTTP API, a function takes three minutes to build a report. What does the client see, and what is the fix?
hint: An HTTP API waits at most 30 seconds.

choices.text: The report, since a Lambda function may run for 15 minutes
choices.why: The function's limit is not the API's; the client gives up at 30 seconds.

choices.text: A `504`; answer `202` with an id and run the work elsewhere
choices.why: Yes. Lessons 20 and 21 build the elsewhere.

choices.text: A `504`; raise the HTTP API's timeout through a quota increase
choices.why: The longer wait AWS added in 2024 is for regional and private REST APIs.

choices.text: A `429`, because the function is busy
choices.why: Busy is not throttling; the integration simply did not answer in time.

prompt: During a load test of the `staging` API, the `prod` API of the same account in São Paulo starts answering `429`. The `prod` function's logs show no throttling. What explains it?
hint: Whose limit is shared by every API in a region?

choices.text: The staging stage's throttle setting applies to every stage
choices.why: A stage's setting is its own.

choices.text: Lambda's concurrency limit, shared with staging's function
choices.why: That would show as throttling on the function, and the logs say there was none.

choices.text: The account-wide API Gateway limit, spent by the test
choices.why: Yes. Every API in the account and region shares 10,000 requests a second.

choices.text: The REST cache filled up and began refusing requests
choices.why: A full cache evicts entries; it does not answer 429.

prompt: moto reported Ana's new 0.5 GB stage cache as `AVAILABLE` at once. What does AWS document?
hint: A cache is a cluster AWS creates for the stage.

choices.text: The same: a cache is ready as soon as the stage setting is saved
choices.why: moto skips the wait; AWS has one.

choices.text: About four minutes in `CREATE_IN_PROGRESS` before it is ready
choices.why: Yes, and it is billed by the hour from then on, hit or not.

choices.text: It is created by the first request that misses, a few seconds later
choices.why: It is created when the stage setting changes, not on traffic.

choices.text: 0.5 GB is below the smallest size
choices.why: 0.5 GB is the smallest size; the largest is 237 GB.

prompt: A shop sells its catalogue API to partners, each with a monthly quota, and also serves its mobile app, whose users sign in and carry a JWT. Which design fits best?
hint: Each audience needs a feature that one kind of API has.

choices.text: One HTTP API for both, with each partner's quota counted inside the function
choices.why: Possible, but it rebuilds usage plans by hand and still lets over-quota calls run the function.

choices.text: REST with usage plans for partners; HTTP with JWT for the app
choices.why: Yes. Each audience gets the API whose feature it needs, and the app pays the lower price.

choices.text: One WebSocket API, so both audiences hear about new products
choices.why: Nothing in the brief needs the server to speak first.

choices.text: One REST API, with an API key for each app user
choices.why: A key identifies, it does not authenticate, and a key per user is a password nobody can change safely.

prompt: 1,000 pages poll an HTTP API every 10 seconds, 8 hours a day, for 22 days. At 1.59 USD per million, what does the month's polling cost?
hint: 8 hours is 28,800 seconds.

prompt: On an HTTP API, the stage called `$___`, with auto-deploy, puts no stage name in the address.
hint: The same word names the WebSocket route for unmatched messages.

prompt: Match each REST integration type with what it does with the request.
hint: One of them never leaves API Gateway.

pairs.right: passes the request to a web server as it came
hands the whole request to a Lambda function
calls another AWS service through a mapping template

right_distractors: runs the request in a container of API Gateway's
